title: Fannie Lou Hamer
hook: a sharecropper beaten for registering voters sings This Little Light of Mine

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mountaintop, and Moses seeing a land he would not enter. Your line was look toward the promised land. What did you do for a future you may not see? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

A bus full of tired people is rolling back from a county courthouse in Mississippi. They have just tried to register to vote, and been turned away. Police stop the bus on a made-up charge. Fear goes through the seats like a draft. And then one woman, a sharecropper who has spent long years in the cotton fields, starts to sing. A church song. Others join in. That woman is Fannie Lou Hamer. That evening the plantation owner tells her to take back her registration or leave. She leaves. Today, a woman who kept singing.

Hamer grew up in the Mississippi Delta, in a family of sharecroppers, and she grew up in church. When young organizers came through asking Black citizens to register to vote, she raised her hand. It cost her the home and the work she had. It cost her more later. Coming back from a voter workshop, she and others were arrested in the town of Winona, and in that jail she was beaten so badly she carried the injuries for the rest of her life. She didn't stop. She sang. Her song was This Little Light of Mine, a gospel song sung in Black churches, and she sang it on buses, in mass meetings, outside courthouses, and, people remember, in jail. The song echoes a saying of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. In the King James Bible: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." And then: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house." A bushel was a basket for measuring grain. Nobody lights a lamp and puts a basket over it. Hamer's little light was not small in the end. She told her story to a committee of a national political convention, on television, and asked out loud whether this was the country it claimed to be. She is remembered for saying she was tired of being tired. She also spoke of loving the people who hurt her, because her faith asked it, and she said so plainly. A small light, in her life, meant one voice that would not go back under the basket.

Here's the practice: sing a small light song. Settle, and breathe. If you know This Little Light of Mine, hum it quietly, or sing one line under your breath. If you know another song about light, use that. If singing isn't for you, light a candle, or switch on a lamp, and just watch it for a while. Notice how a small flame fills a dark room. Then think of one good thing you've been keeping under a basket. If you pray, you can hold Jesus's words: ye are the light of the world. The bell holds the time.
Fannie Lou Hamer. A Mississippi sharecropper who lost her home and was beaten for registering to vote, and kept singing This Little Light of Mine.
Your line: this little light. Today, take one good thing out from under the basket and let it be seen, not for praise, but so it gives light to the house. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Black churches in the United States sing This Little Light of Mine in worship, and it was sung at mass meetings and marches of the civil rights movement.
